title: Invocatio
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 fb3fdb1d8a4a3b82. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: The four lines with which the Metamorphoses opens. Ovid names his subject — shapes changed into new bodies — asks the gods to favour the undertaking, and asks for one continuous song running from the world's first beginning down to his own day. The edition of record sets these lines off as their own section before the creation of the world begins. The promise made here is the poem's whole architecture: not a collection of separate tales but a single unbroken thread, and every transformation that follows answers to it.

sentences.t:
In nova fert animus mutatas dicere formas
corpora; di, coeptis (nam vos mutastis et illas)
adspirate meis primaque ab origine mundi
ad mea perpetuum deducite tempora carmen.
sentences.l:
Of shapes changed into new
bodies my spirit moves me to tell; gods, on my beginnings —
for you changed these too — breathe favour, and from the world's first origin
draw a continuous song down to my own times.
sentences.i: My spirit moves me to tell of shapes transformed into new bodies. Gods, breathe favour on what I begin — you worked these changes too — and spin out an unbroken song from the world's first beginning down to my own day.
sentences.n: The enjambment is the point: 'in nova' hangs at the end of line 1 with nothing to agree with, and does not find its noun ('corpora') until line 2 — the change happens across the line break. 'fert animus' = 'the spirit carries (me)', an idiom for an impulse one does not choose. 'coeptis… meis' is dative with 'adspirate' ('breathe upon my beginnings'), the wind-in-the-sails metaphor Latin uses for divine favour. 'deducite' is a weaving word — to draw out a fine thread — and the claim it makes is programmatic: a 'carmen deductum', a finely spun song, in the manner Callimachus made fashionable, even though what follows runs to fifteen books of hexameter.
